briefing.text: Mutations in the histone acetyltransferase genes are a competing cause of histone acetylation differences. p300 (EP300) and CBP (CREBBP) are the enzymes that write H3 K18/K27 and H2B N-terminal acetylation, which are the same sites given priority for the Wnt test. The library reports EP300 mutated in roughly 7 percent of endometrial carcinomas, CREBBP also recurrently, and in other tumour types these mutations cluster in high-mutation-burden / MSI tumours (literature figures; confirm the counts in this cohort). If such mutations are unevenly spread between Wnt-active and Wnt-inactive tumours they can create or hide a Wnt association. Check: from data_mutations.txt flag tumours with truncating mutations, or missense mutations in the HAT or bromodomain, in EP300 or CREBBP (note KAT2A, KAT2B, HDAC1-3 if any); cross-tabulate the flag against CTNNB1 exon 3 hotspot status and GENOMICS_SUBTYPE; test whether flagged tumours differ in the p300/CBP-type histone sites. If they do, or if the flag is unbalanced across Wnt groups, rerun the Wnt test with HAT-mutant tumours excluded or with HAT-mutation status as a covariate, and do not report a HAT-mutation effect as a Wnt effect.
briefing.reason: A confounder not covered by the earlier briefing: it acts on exactly the histone sites the team was told to prioritise, and it is tied to hypermutated subtypes, so it can change both the Wnt effect estimate and its interpretation.

briefing.text: Proliferation rate as a hidden driver of bulk histone acetyl signals. Newly synthesised histone H4 is diacetylated at K5 and K12 (by HAT1) before replication-coupled deposition and deacetylated within about an hour, and histone protein synthesis is S-phase coupled, so H4 K5/K12 acetylation and histone abundance rise with the fraction of cycling cells. A Wnt-versus-histone-acetylation association, or its absence, can therefore reflect how fast the Wnt-active tumours proliferate rather than Wnt-directed acetylation (the library notes CTNNB1-mutant tumours are mostly low-grade; confirm in this cohort). Check: build a proliferation score from data_mrna_seq_rsem.txt (mean across-sample z-score of those present of MKI67, TOP2A, PCNA, MCM2-7, CCNB1, BUB1), or use MKI67/PCNA/MCM protein from data_protein_quantification.txt; correlate it with each histone acetyl site; compare it between Wnt groups; also compare HISTOLOGIC_GRADE_FIGO between Wnt groups. If proliferation relates to both, add the proliferation score (and grade) as a covariate in site ~ Wnt and report the adjusted effect alongside the unadjusted one. Interpret H4 N-terminal K5/K8/K12 sites separately from the p300/CBP-type marks (H3 K18/K27, H2B N-terminus): only the latter are the expected beta-catenin readout, the former are the ones most exposed to proliferation.
briefing.reason: A second confounder not in the earlier briefing; it specifically affects H4 tail sites, which the earlier briefing put in the priority set, so it changes which covariates are needed and how H4 results are read.

briefing.text: Choice of per-site test with a small Wnt-active group. CTNNB1 hotspot mutants are expected to be a minority of the roughly 95 tumours (confirm both numbers), and TMT log-ratios are heavy-tailed. Under those conditions a per-site Student t-test or Pearson correlation is fragile: the t-test is robust to non-normality only when groups are not small and there are no outliers, per-site variance estimates from few samples are erratic, and one or two extreme tumours can create or destroy a Pearson correlation between a Wnt score and an acetyl site. Do this: use a Welch (unequal-variance) test or a moderated linear model (limma-style, which accepts covariates such as subtype, plex, purity and tolerates NA without imputation) as the primary per-site test; for the top sites also run Wilcoxon rank-sum (binary Wnt status) and Spearman (continuous Wnt score) and require agreement in direction and rough significance; plot the values by group and check group variances; redo the test leaving out each of the most extreme samples and discard any association that disappears when a single sample is removed. Because the Wnt-active group is small, add the covariates from the other briefing items one at a time or in small sets as sensitivity analyses instead of all in one model, and report how the Wnt effect moves under each.
briefing.reason: Fixes the statistical method for the primary test: with few Wnt-active samples the default t-test/Pearson can flip the conclusion on one or two outlying tumours, in either direction.

shared_assumptions: Both teams read 'Wnt signaling' as two variables only: CTNNB1 exon-3 hotspot mutation and a Wnt-target mRNA score. Neither tested a Wnt readout that is independent of the mutation call and of mRNA (beta-catenin protein abundance, its phosphosites), so 'Wnt signaling' and 'carrying a CTNNB1 hotspot' were never separated; team A's own finding that the score does not track the top H2B sites among wild-type tumours points at this gap.

Both teams assumed that a significant global/set test for the Wnt variable is evidence about Wnt specifically. Each compared histone sites with non-histone sites (specificity across sites), but neither asked how the same test behaves for other predictors with a similar subtype distribution (other driver mutations, the pathway-activity columns in the sample table, random gene-set scores). Both found the non-histone acetylome also shifts with Wnt status, so a predictor-side null was needed and not run.

Both teams pooled every row with a histone gene symbol into one 'histone acetylation' family: core histone tails together with linker H1 (34 of 136 rows), macroH2A (20 rows) and H2A variants. Neither showed which class carries the global signal; team B reports macroH2A acetylation moving with Wnt and macroH2A protein abundance explaining part of it.

Both teams applied the same >=50%-observed filter, which removes about 55 of 136 histone rows, and treated the remaining rows as the histone acetylome. Missingness is plex-structured and Wnt mutants are unevenly spread over batches, so the retained set could differ systematically from the dropped set.

Both teams treated tumours as exchangeable in label permutations at most within batch or subtype. The measurement unit is a TMT plex (16 plexes of 4-8 tumours); neither ran a permutation restricted to plexes, and team A adjusted only at batch level.

Both teams treated paralog-labelled H2B N-terminal rows (HIST1H2BB / HIST1H2BM / HIST2H2BF / HIST1H2BD / HIST1H2BL / HIST3H2BB, K6-K25) as separate sites apart from exact duplicates. If these are the same peptides re-labelled, the conclusion of both teams rests on very few independent measurements.
unused_evidence: data_phosphoprotein_quantification.txt holds CTNNB1 S33, S37, T41, S45 (degron), S552, S675 and GSK3B S9/S21 rows; data_protein_quantification.txt holds CTNNB1, AXIN1, NKD1, NOTUM, LEF1, TCF7 protein rows. The library named 'CTNNB1 protein/phosphosites' as Wnt variables, yet neither team used them as a Wnt readout.

data_protein_quantification.txt holds H2B rows HIST1H2BA, HIST1H2BJ and HIST3H2BB plus many other histone rows (H1, H2A, H3, H4, macroH2A). Team B said the top H2B sites have no matched protein; team A used one paralog. A composite histone-abundance covariate was not built by either.

data_clinical_sample.txt has 11 PATHWAY_ACTIVITY_* scores (EGFR, Hypoxia, JAK.STAT, MAPK, NFkB, PI3K, TGFb, TNFa, Trail, VEGF, p53; no Wnt column), a STEMNESS_SCORE and ER/PR scores. These could serve as comparison predictors to show whether the histone-acetylation association is particular to Wnt; unused for that purpose.
PROTEOMICS_TMT_PLEX and PROTEOMICS_TMT_CHANNEL: plex was used as a covariate by team B and only as batch by team A; neither used it as the permutation block.

data_cna.txt / data_log2cna.txt (copy number of the histone gene clusters and of EP300/CREBBP), data_methylation_epic.txt (promoter methylation of Wnt antagonists), miRNA and circular RNA tables were not used. These are probably peripheral to the hypothesis, but copy number of the histone clusters is a possible driver of histone abundance in CNV-high tumours.

Acetyl rows on the acetylation machinery and on Wnt components (EP300 and CREBBP auto-acetylation loop sites, CTNNB1-K666/K671, BCL9, TCF7L2, TLE1/3) exist; both teams treated them as background or context, in line with the library's advice that they are not histone acetylation.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A: the H2B protein adjustment used a single paralog (HIST3H2BB) as stand-in; reported, not resolved. This matters because team A's whole conclusion was moved onto the H2B N-terminal sites after the H3/H4 differences were explained by protein abundance.
Team A: plex adjusted only at batch level and plots never inspected; reported, not resolved.

Team A: no dose-response among wild-type tumours (rho 0.0-0.09 between Wnt score and top H2B sites); competitive test not significant within CNV-low (p=0.17); purity adjustment halves the nominal hits. Reported, not resolved.
Team B: the CTNNB1-mutation association disappears after matched histone-protein adjustment (p=0.32) and the top H2B sites were left unadjusted; reported, not resolved.

Team B: no significant association within CNV-low or within endometrioid MSS non-POLE, and the batch x subtype stratified permutation for mutation gives p=0.06; reported as underpowered, not resolved.

The two teams disagree on the same stratum: within CNV-low team A reports permutation p=0.03 for the hotspot contrast, team B p=0.28 (and 0.12 for the score). Different statistics and covariates, but the disagreement shows the within-subtype result depends on analyst choices.
second_readings: 'Relationship' can mean any cohort-wide statistical association (which a between-subtype difference would satisfy) or an association that holds for tumours of the same subtype. Both teams leaned on the stricter reading for their checks but took the label from the cohort-wide adjusted test; under the strict reading the within-subtype evidence is mixed.

'Wnt signaling' can mean pathway activity (graded, in every tumour) or genetic activation by CTNNB1 mutation. The evidence is stronger for the mRNA score in team B and for the mutant-versus-wild-type contrast in team A, and team A found no graded relation among wild-type tumours.

'Histone acetylation' can mean acetylation of core histone tails (the usual sense), acetylation on any histone-family protein including linker H1 and macroH2A, or the histone-acetylation process as a gene set (acetyltransferases, deacetylases and their own modification state), as in a pathway-enrichment result. Both teams used the second sense only.
Scale: relative site abundance versus acetylation stoichiometry (site relative to histone amount). The answer differs by scale for H3/H4 sites in both teams' own results.
Group: all 95 tumours versus endometrioid tumours only (no serous tumour carries a hotspot mutation).
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust in the agreed label, not high: both teams see a cohort-wide association that survives subtype, batch and purity adjustment, but it is set-level only, weakens or disappears within the CNV-low subtype and after histone-protein adjustment, and the two teams disagree on the same stratum. The questions test whether the signal is specific to Wnt, independent of TMT plex and histone abundance, and carried by more than a handful of H2B peptides; if it fails those, the label needs to be reconsidered.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your set test shows that histone sites differ by Wnt status, and you also found the non-histone acetylome differs. Run the identical histone set test (same sites, same statistic, same permutation and subtype stratification) with other predictors in place of Wnt: (a) hotspot or loss-of-function status of a few other recurrent drivers with comparable group sizes, (b) each PATHWAY_ACTIVITY_* score in data_clinical_sample.txt, (c) a few hundred scores built from random 10-gene mRNA sets. Report where the Wnt mutation and the Wnt score fall in that distribution of statistics. Does the result change how you read your set-test p-value, or the method you rest the label on?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You adjusted for TMT structure at batch level only. Tabulate CTNNB1 hotspot status by PROTEOMICS_TMT_PLEX (16 plexes), then rerun the set test and the top H2B-site tests with Wnt labels permuted only within plex (or with plex as a blocking factor), and look at the per-plex plots of the top H2B sites that you did not inspect. Does the association hold within plexes, and does the result change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your conclusion rests on H2B N-terminal sites adjusted for one stand-in protein row (HIST3H2BB). Check two things in the data: (1) how HIST3H2BB protein correlates with the other H2B rows in the protein table (HIST1H2BA, HIST1H2BJ) and with a composite of all core-histone protein rows, and whether the H2B sites still differ by Wnt status when adjusted for that composite; (2) the pairwise correlations among the H2B N-terminal acetyl rows across paralog labels (HIST1H2BB, HIST1H2BM, HIST2H2BF, HIST1H2BD, HIST1H2BL, HIST3H2BB), to state how many independent measurements carry the signal. Does either result change the method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You found no relation between the Wnt score and the top H2B sites among wild-type tumours, so the evidence so far is for the hotspot contrast rather than for graded Wnt activity. The protein and phosphoprotein tables hold CTNNB1 protein abundance and CTNNB1 phosphosite rows, which you were told are Wnt variables but did not use. Check whether they track hotspot status and the mRNA score (positive control), then test them against the histone sites in all tumours and among wild-type tumours only. Does a Wnt readout that is not the mutation call and not mRNA give the same answer, and does that change the method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your Freedman-Lane global test shows histone sites associate with the Wnt score after adjustment, and you also found excess signal in non-histone sites. Run the identical global test (same 79 sites, same covariate sets) with other predictors in place of Wnt: (a) each PATHWAY_ACTIVITY_* score in data_clinical_sample.txt, (b) a few hundred scores built from random mRNA gene sets of the same size as your Wnt set, (c) mutation status of a few other recurrent drivers with comparable group sizes. Report where the Wnt score and the CTNNB1 hotspot fall in that distribution. Does the result change how you read the global p-value, or the method you rest the label on?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You left the top H2B sites out of the protein-abundance adjustment for lack of a matched protein, and the mutation association vanished in the 41 sites you could adjust. The protein table does contain H2B rows (HIST1H2BA, HIST1H2BJ, HIST3H2BB) and many other histone rows. Check how these rows correlate with one another and with the H2B acetyl sites, build a histone-abundance covariate that covers all 79 sites, and rerun the global test for both Wnt definitions. Does the association survive when every site is adjusted, and does that change the method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your 79 sites mix core histone tails with linker H1, macroH2A and H2A-variant rows, and you report macroH2A moving with Wnt. Split the sites by class (core H2A/H2B/H3/H4 tails; linker H1; macroH2A and other variants), collapse rows that are the same peptide under different paralog labels (check pairwise correlations among the H2B N-terminal rows), and rerun the adjusted global test per class. Which class carries the signal, how many independent measurements is that, and does the result change the method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: The >=50%-observed filter removed more than 50 of the 136 histone acetyl rows, missingness follows TMT plex, and CTNNB1 mutants are concentrated in one batch. Check (1) whether being observed or missing for the dropped sites is itself related to Wnt status once plex is accounted for, (2) which histone residues are in the dropped set, and (3) whether the global test changes when the threshold is loosened with a minimum count per Wnt group and when Wnt labels are permuted within plex rather than within batch. Does any of these change the method?

In isobaric-tag (TMT) acetyl-lysine enrichment proteomics as processed by common large-consortium pipelines, how is an acetylated peptide that maps to several histone paralogues (for example the H2B N-terminal tail) assigned a gene symbol and site label: can one peptide quantification appear as separate rows under different paralog names or different lysine positions, and are the reported site-level log ratios normalised to parent-protein abundance or not?
questions.why: Both teams rest their conclusion on H2B N-terminal rows listed under several paralog symbols and on whether the signal survives protein-abundance adjustment; the answer fixes how many independent measurements there are and whether further protein adjustment is needed.

questions.question: For multi-plex TMT experiments with a common reference channel and plex-structured missing values, what do methods papers recommend for permutation or resampling tests of a sample-level variable: are samples exchangeable across plexes, or should labels be permuted within plex (restricted permutation / blocking), and how should sites missing in whole plexes be handled?
questions.why: Both teams' primary evidence is a sample-label permutation test; neither permuted within plex, and the validity of the reported p-values depends on the exchangeability unit.

questions.question: Which protein-level and phosphosite-level measurements are accepted readouts of canonical Wnt/beta-catenin pathway activity in bulk tumour proteomics (total beta-catenin abundance, phosphorylation at S33/S37/T41/S45, S552, S675, GSK3B S9), and when a tumour carries a missense mutation inside the beta-catenin degron, are the degron phosphopeptides from the mutant allele still identified and quantified by standard reference-database searches or only those from the wild-type allele?
questions.why: Neither team used a Wnt readout independent of the mutation call and mRNA; before the teams use beta-catenin protein and phosphosite rows they need to know which sites indicate activity and whether degron-site values are biased in mutant tumours.

findings.question: In isobaric-tag (TMT) acetyl-lysine enrichment proteomics as processed by common large-consortium pipelines, how is an acetylated peptide that maps to several histone paralogues (for example the H2B N-terminal tail) assigned a gene symbol and site label: can one peptide quantification appear as separate rows under different paralog names or different lysine positions, and are the reported site-level log ratios normalised to parent-protein abundance or not?
findings.answer: Partly settled. (1) Row construction: in the Broad Spectrum Mill route used for consortium TMT acetylomes, the site table has one row per variable-modification (VM) site; PSMs are merged into a single row for all non-conflicting observations of that site (different missed-cleavage forms, precursor charges, confident and ambiguous localisations), and the PTM site reports use the 'unexpand subgroups' protein grouping (the proteome uses 'expand subgroups, top uses shared'). By design, then, a peptide shared by paralogues is reported once under one representative accession of its protein group, not once per paralogue. Separate rows still legitimately arise for (a) different acetyl-site combinations of the same tail peptide (each mono/di/tri-acetyl form is its own row; these overlap chemically and are strongly correlated) and (b) paralogue-specific peptide sequences (H2B variants differ at a few N-terminal residues, so rows under different H2B gene symbols can be different peptides from the same histone family; this sequence point is background knowledge, not read on the web). (2) Other pipelines differ: the PDC common data analysis pipeline uses MS-GF+, PhosphoRS and a 'generalized parsimony' gene roll-up, and downstream resources re-annotate sites to chosen isoforms and recompute positions, so gene symbol and lysine number can be relabelled. The web therefore does NOT settle whether the teams' table duplicates one peptide quantification under several paralog symbols; that has to be checked in the table itself (rows with correlation near 1 and identical missing-value pattern are one measurement and should be collapsed; count independent peptides, not rows, and treat paralog symbols as histone-family labels). (3) Normalisation: site values are log2 ratios to the common reference with sample-level normalisation only. No pipeline description read includes normalisation to parent-protein abundance, and PTM methods reviews state that protein abundance must be assessed separately, so protein adjustment by the analyst is still needed and is not a double correction. Caveat: the Spectrum Mill wording was read in search excerpts of methods sections; the pages opened with the contents tool were cut off before their Methods sections.

findings.question: For multi-plex TMT experiments with a common reference channel and plex-structured missing values, what do methods papers recommend for permutation or resampling tests of a sample-level variable: are samples exchangeable across plexes, or should labels be permuted within plex (restricted permutation / blocking), and how should sites missing in whole plexes be handled?
findings.answer: No TMT-specific methods paper on permutation exchangeability was found, so this is the general permutation principle applied to plexes. Permutation tests are valid only if observations are exchangeable under the null. Where data have a block structure, the permutation literature (Winkler et al. 2014 and 2015) says to use only rearrangements that respect it: permute within block (within-block exchangeability) or shuffle whole blocks, and deal with nuisance variables by permuting residuals. For multi-plex TMT, the plex is the natural exchangeability block: samples in a plex share the same peptide selection, reference-channel denominator and missingness. Labels should therefore be permuted within plex, or plex should enter the model as a nuisance or blocking term. Unrestricted permutation across plexes is valid only if plex affects neither the values nor the missingness, which is false for sites missing in whole plexes. TMT statistics papers do not use sample permutation: MSstatsTMT fits linear mixed-effects models with mixture (plex) as a random effect and tolerates missing values; msTrawler models between-batch differences in the number and quality of observations 'without relying on unverifiable imputations or discarding reliable measurements'. For sites missing in whole plexes: do not impute; test on the observed plexes only; permute within plex, which keeps the missingness pattern and per-group sample counts of every permuted data set equal to the observed one; and require a minimum number of informative plexes (plexes that contain both groups). The teams' unrestricted permutation p-values should be re-run with within-plex permutation before being relied on.

findings.question: Which protein-level and phosphosite-level measurements are accepted readouts of canonical Wnt/beta-catenin pathway activity in bulk tumour proteomics (total beta-catenin abundance, phosphorylation at S33/S37/T41/S45, S552, S675, GSK3B S9), and when a tumour carries a missense mutation inside the beta-catenin degron, are the degron phosphopeptides from the mutant allele still identified and quantified by standard reference-database searches or only those from the wild-type allele?
findings.answer: Readouts: phosphorylation of the beta-catenin N-terminal degron (CK1alpha primes S45, then GSK3beta phosphorylates T41, S37 and S33, creating the beta-TrCP docking site) marks the protein for ubiquitylation and proteasomal degradation. Phospho-S33/S37/T41/S45 is therefore a destruction (pathway-off) mark; Wnt activation appears as loss of this phosphorylation with accumulation and nuclear translocation of beta-catenin. S552 (AKT) and S675 (PKA) are alternative phosphorylations that 'may enhance' beta-catenin activity, but they are driven by PI3K/AKT and cAMP/PKA signalling and are not specific to canonical Wnt. The pages read did not address GSK3B S9 or how well total beta-catenin in bulk tissue tracks Wnt activity, so the web did not settle those two. Background knowledge, not verified here: GSK3B S9 is an AKT-type inhibitory site that is not required for Wnt signalling, and total beta-catenin in bulk tissue is dominated by the junctional, cadherin-bound pool; both are weak readouts, and target-gene expression remains the accepted one. Mutant allele: standard database searches identify only peptides present in the reference protein database; single-amino-acid-variant peptides are 'usually not present in the database and therefore not identified' unless a customised variant database is searched. All exon 3 hotspot codons (32 to 45) lie on one tryptic peptide (about residues 20 to 49; sequence from background knowledge). In a degron-mutant tumour, degron phosphosite rows from a reference search therefore report only the wild-type allele (plus non-tumour cells), not the stabilised mutant protein, and several hotspot mutations remove the phospho-acceptor residue itself. Degron phosphosite values are thus systematically biased in mutant tumours and should not be used there as a Wnt readout independent of the mutation call. Total beta-catenin protein is quantified from peptides outside the degron, so it includes both alleles.
